title: The Amazon Rainforest
content:
The Amazon Rainforest, often referred to as the 'lungs of the Earth', spans across nine countries in South America and covers approximately 5.5 million square kilometres. It is home to an estimated 10% of all species on the planet, making it the most biodiverse place on Earth.

The forest floor receives less than 2% of the sunlight that hits the canopy above. Despite this, the rainforest teems with life at every level. Jaguars prowl the undergrowth, while howler monkeys swing through the mid-canopy and harpy eagles soar above the treetops.

Deforestation poses the greatest threat to this ecosystem. Between 2001 and 2020, the Amazon lost roughly 8% of its total forest cover. Scientists warn that if deforestation reaches a tipping point of 20-25%, the rainforest could begin converting into savannah, with devastating consequences for global climate regulation.

title: The Great Barrier Reef
content:
Stretching over 2,300 kilometres along Australia's northeastern coast, the Great Barrier Reef is the largest living structure on Earth — so vast it can be seen from space. Composed of nearly 3,000 individual reef systems, it supports an extraordinary array of marine life.

The reef is built by tiny organisms called coral polyps, which secrete calcium carbonate to form hard skeletons. Over thousands of years, these skeletons accumulate to create the massive structures we see today. The vibrant colours of coral come from symbiotic algae called zooxanthellae that live within the coral tissue.

Rising ocean temperatures have triggered mass coral bleaching events with increasing frequency. When water temperatures rise even 1-2 degrees above the summer maximum, corals expel their zooxanthellae, turning white. If conditions do not improve within weeks, the coral dies. The 2016 and 2017 bleaching events affected over two-thirds of the reef.

title: The Wanderer's Return
content:
I left these shores when skies were grey,
With nothing but a worn-out bag,
Through desert sands and mountain clay,
My spirit never once did sag.

I crossed the seas where dolphins play,
And slept beneath the southern stars,
I learned the words the wind would say,
And bore the journey's countless scars.

Now standing where I once began,
The same old oak, the same stone wall,
I see it all with wiser span —
That home was here through it all.

title: Climate Change and Food Security
content:
Climate change is already affecting global food production in complex and sometimes contradictory ways. While increased CO2 levels can boost plant growth — a phenomenon known as the 'CO2 fertilisation effect' — the accompanying rise in temperatures and changing rainfall patterns often negate these benefits.

Wheat yields are projected to decline by 6% for every degree Celsius of global warming. Rice paddies in Southeast Asia face increasing threats from saltwater intrusion as sea levels rise. Meanwhile, extreme weather events — droughts, floods, and heatwaves — are becoming more frequent and severe, devastating harvests without warning.

Adaptation strategies include developing heat-resistant crop varieties, improving irrigation efficiency, and diversifying food sources. Some farmers are turning to ancient grains like teff and millet, which are naturally more resilient to harsh conditions than modern wheat and rice varieties.
